clue.text: One who invents wraps worn by the trendy

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the things the trendy wear

parts.note: a person who devises new products or styles
wraps are garments, things we put on

explanation.surface: An inventor's line of shawls and stoles has become popular with the fashionable set.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: what is 'worn by the trendy' is branded fashion, and the wordplay builds it from a maker plus garments.
explanation.definitionFit: Labels from famous fashion houses are what style-conscious people put on, so the phrase describes them.

clue.text: Freshly dead cub he abandoned

indicators.note: something done freshly is made anew, so the letters are made into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A lion cub has just died, left behind by its father.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abandoned' reads as deserted, but here it means morally dissolute.
explanation.definitionFit: Abandoned in the sense of wildly unrestrained in behaviour matches someone corrupted by excess and vice.

clue.text: Kirk body's yielding, it's said

indicators.note: something said is heard rather than read, so we want a word that is pronounced like the one meant

parts.note: cession is the act of yielding or ceding, for instance territory

explanation.surface: A church body is giving way, people say.
explanation.walkthrough: The kirk session is the governing court of a local Church of Scotland congregation, made up of minister and elders.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scottish Presbyterian churches the minister and elders form the local governing court, called by this name.

clue.text: Doctor examining larynx, too brightly lit inside

parts.note: surface padding: it sets the medical scene and gives no letters

indicators.note: inside tells us the answer is lying within the run of words written in front of it

parts.note: found across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A doctor peers at a patient's throat, which is lit up too harshly inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' only sets the scene: the letters run from examininG into LARYnx.
explanation.definitionFit: Glary describes light that is dazzling or excessive, like a harsh lamp shone into a throat.

clue.text: Makes slow progress along borders

explanation.surface: Someone creeps gradually along the boundaries of a field.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means moving bit by bit; as a plural noun it names the outer margins of something.

clue.text: Lance broken on head requiring antisepsis

indicators.note: a broken thing is in pieces, which can be put back together in another order

parts.note: letters to be rearranged
a ness is a headland, a promontory

explanation.surface: A medical lance has snapped on someone's head, so the wound needs sterilising.
explanation.walkthrough: Ness, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness, is a place-name word for a headland.
explanation.definitionFit: Antisepsis is keeping wounds free of germs, which amounts to being free of dirt and infection.

clue.text: Have greater force than published edition

parts.note: a book that is out has been released
an issue of a magazine is a number

explanation.surface: A newly released edition carries more weight than the earlier one.
explanation.definitionFit: To be more numerous than an opponent is to have the bigger force or army on your side.

clue.text: Spanish lady made secret cache of seaweed, maybe

parts.note: concealed something away
seaweed is one example of an alga

explanation.surface: A Spanish woman tucked away a private store, of seaweed perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidalga is a Spanish noblewoman, the female equivalent of a hidalgo, a member of the minor gentry.

clue.text: Throw over disheartened lady with diffidence

indicators.note: losing its heart means the middle letters of the word are taken out

parts.note: to shy is to toss, as at a coconut shy
the word with its central letters removed

explanation.surface: Someone tosses something over a downcast woman, timidly.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, 'over' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something with diffidence means doing it timidly and without self-confidence, the adverb for bashful.

clue.text: Add sparkle to bracelet — second sight's involved

indicators.note: something involved is caught up inside something else, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a rigid bracelet
extrasensory perception; the 's stands for has

explanation.surface: A clairvoyant's gift makes a piece of jewellery glitter.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after sight is 'has': second sight has got involved with the bracelet.
explanation.definitionFit: To bespangle is to cover with glittering ornaments, which makes something shine and dazzle.

clue.text: Time to whirl popular toy

parts.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
a swirling current of water or air

explanation.surface: It is time to spin a favourite plaything.
explanation.definitionFit: The stuffed bear named after Theodore Roosevelt is one of the best-loved children's playthings.

clue.text: Single-mindedness of army group on enemy's tail

parts.note: a military formation

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: only the closing letter is used

explanation.surface: A detachment of soldiers pursues its foe with fixed purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: Unity is oneness of aim and purpose, everyone in agreement with a shared goal.

clue.text: Awfully sullen, say, in a lewd fashion

indicators.note: done awfully means done badly, so the letters come out in a mangled order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sulks terribly, while behaving indecently, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example' but is simply part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting in a fleshly, physically indulgent manner is close in sense to behaving lewdly.

clue.text: Get away from jail when cell's left open

indicators.note: the answer is laid open to view within the words written, not concealed by any change

parts.note: runs from the second letter of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A prisoner seizes the chance to escape when the cell door has been left unlocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From jail' simply completes the picture of an escape; the letters sit inside wHEN CEll's.
explanation.definitionFit: Hence used as an old imperative means go away from here, a command to leave.

clue.text: Object about clique being under siege

indicators.note: about means going round, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: an end is an aim or object
a closed social set

explanation.surface: A target surrounded by an exclusive set finds itself besieged.
explanation.definitionFit: A besieged town is surrounded on all sides by enemy forces, hemmed in completely.

clue.text: Derby gear designed for old fellow

indicators.note: something designed is newly arranged to a plan, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Racegoing outfits have been made for an elderly gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derby is the famous English flat race at Epsom, where smart dress is traditional.
explanation.definitionFit: A man with a white or grizzled beard is a familiar picture of age, so the word means an old man.

clue.text: Final wish for cooked hot dog laced with gin fizz

indicators.note: cooked food is altered, so the letters are worked into a new form
a fizz is a bubbling commotion, so the combined letters are stirred together

parts.note: first group of letters
added to the first group

explanation.surface: A last-orders snack: a sausage roll served with a gin fizz.
explanation.walkthrough: A gin fizz is a cocktail, which hides that both words are working: gin is fodder, fizz stirs it.
explanation.definitionFit: The parting words said at the end of an evening or before sleep are a last wish to someone.

clue.text: Top of dome is part of gas-lamp to take to bits

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down answer is its opening letter, so only that one is used

parts.note: the first letter only
taken as written
the mesh hood that glows over a gas flame

explanation.surface: The cap of a dome-shaped gas light is a component you remove to take the lamp apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Dismantling something means taking it apart piece by piece, reducing it to its components.

clue.text: Tasty food shop gets 100 promises to pay

parts.note: short for delicatessen
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
an IOU is a written acknowledgement of a debt

explanation.surface: A grocer selling tasty fare receives a hundred notes of credit.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe food that is very pleasant to eat, full of flavour.

clue.text: Internal organ absorbs most of fresh tonic

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its final letter is used
to absorb something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: the large organ that filters the blood
fresh means new, cut short by one letter

explanation.surface: An organ of the body soaks up nearly all of a refreshing pick-me-up.
explanation.walkthrough: A livener is an informal word for a drink that perks you up, often an early one.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonic is anything that invigorates, and a livener is a pick-me-up drink that does just that.

clue.text: Where businesses conceal message in pictures

indicators.note: to conceal is to keep something inside out of sight, so the answer is tucked within these words

parts.note: runs across the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: Companies hide their slogans in images.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebus is a puzzle that spells out words or a phrase with images and symbols instead of letters.

clue.text: Yeti-like creature's vast base

parts.note: very large
the bottom of something, as at the foot of a hill

explanation.surface: The abominable snowman stands on enormous feet.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is': the creature is a vast base.
explanation.definitionFit: Bigfoot, or Sasquatch, is the hairy ape-man of North American legend, a cousin of the Himalayan yeti.

clue.text: Foolish chatter in hoax calls

parts.note: to have someone on is to fool them
rings someone on the telephone

explanation.surface: Prank phone calls are full of silly talk.
explanation.walkthrough: To haver is a Scots word for talking nonsense, so haverings is idle or foolish talk.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scottish usage the noun means rambling, nonsensical talk, which is foolish chatter.

clue.text: Man at top of high moorland

parts.note: the male pronoun
taken as written

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down answer is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the first letter only

explanation.surface: A man stands at the summit of upland moor.
explanation.definitionFit: Heath is open uncultivated land covered with heather and scrub, much like a moor.

clue.text: She's thrifty except for early sign of rashness

definitions.note: a clause describing the person the noun names

parts.note: save meaning but or except

indicators.note: the early sign of a word is its opening letter, so only that is taken

parts.note: the first letter only

explanation.surface: A woman is careful with money apart from the odd impulsive splurge.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who puts money aside and spends carefully is a thrifty person, a careful economiser.

clue.text: Light boat with most of fodder for Hebridean isle

indicators.note: most of a word means everything except its last letter is used

parts.note: a gig is a light, narrow rowing boat
hay, cut short by one letter

explanation.surface: A small boat carries a load of animal feed out to a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: Gigha is a small island off the west coast of Kintyre in Scotland, usually counted with the Inner Hebrides.
explanation.definitionFit: Gigha lies in the Inner Hebrides island group off western Scotland, so it fits as an isle there.

clue.text: Damage nets catching animal like a cat

indicators.note: these words catch and hold the answer within them

parts.note: runs across the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: Torn nets trap a wild feline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Damage' looks like an anagram signal for nets, but it is the start of the run of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The genet is a slender spotted carnivore of Africa and southern Europe, related to the civet and catlike in form.

clue.text: Abolish yearbook, taking out first of almanacs

indicators.note: taking something out removes it, so a letter is dropped
the first of a word is its opening letter, which is the one to drop

parts.note: a book published once a year
its first letter

explanation.surface: Scrap the yearly publication, removing the top almanac from the series.
explanation.definitionFit: To annul is to declare void or cancel, the same as abolishing a law or arrangement.

clue.text: Nearly finished making an announcement

definitions.meaning: first meaning: failing, running out, as of supplies or strength
second meaning: declaring or making known publicly

explanation.surface: Someone almost done with a task is making a public statement.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both breaking down or running out, and declaring something publicly.

clue.text: Handle no longer opening Parliament's doors

definitions.text: Handle no longer opening Parliament's doors

parts.words: Handle no longer opening Parliament's doors
parts.note: surface reading: a door handle that has stopped working at Westminster
setter's reading: a handle is slang for a name or form of address, here a peerage passed down through a family, which since 1999 no longer gives an automatic seat in the House of Lords

explanation.surface: A worn-out door handle at Westminster no longer lets anyone in.
explanation.walkthrough: The House of Lords Act 1999 removed most peers who sat by right of birth, so an inherited rank stopped opening Parliament's doors.
explanation.definitionFit: A handle is slang for a name or rank, and inherited peerages lost their automatic right to sit in the Lords.
